extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory and American history
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of republican durability and commerce
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and synthesis of Tocqueville's criteria for the durability of republican institutions, the (accidental) nature of the Union, causes of American commercial/maritime success, and barriers to aristocracy. Useful for scholars or students evaluating why political forms persist or change and what drives national commercial power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union versus republic durability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union is accidental and will last only while circumstances favor it; the republican form of government has a much deeper foundation and greater prospect of permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville contrasts the fragility of a political Union (which one revolution or a change in public opinion might destroy) with the deeper-rooted character of republican institutions that are grounded in laws, manners, and opinions; thus evaluate institutional durability by distinguishing accidental political unions from underlying republican culture and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and features of a republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: A republican government is 'the slow and quiet action of society upon itself'—a regular state founded on the enlightened will of the people, conciliatory in character, allowing resolutions time to ripen, deliberately discussed and executed with mature judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a government is truly republican, look for deliberation, gradual social influence, respect for morality and religion, and institutions that permit measured decision-making rather than sudden autocratic impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on the power of the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the majority is not unlimited: in the moral world humanity, justice, and reason enjoy supremacy, and in the political world vested rights must be treated with deference; the majority recognizes these two barriers though it may sometimes overstep them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate majoritarian rule not merely by numerical dominance but by whether it acknowledges and respects moral principles and preexisting vested rights; breaches indicate demagogic tendencies and institutional weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagoguery as an anti-pattern in republicanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A corrupted republicanism becomes 'the rule of those who are strenuous partisans of the majority'—not the people themselves but leaders claiming to act for them—thereby disregarding rights and moral obligations and justifying 'legitimate tyranny' in the name of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for rhetorical claims of speaking for 'the people' used to bypass consultation, to despise traditional moral limits, or to legitimize abuses; such patterns signal departure from healthy republican norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of republican principles requires long, consistent opposing causes to change
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but a long series of events, all having the same tendency, can substitute republican laws, opinions, and manners with an opposite mass; in practice, the republic will not perish quickly but only after laborious, often-interrupted social processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prospects for systemic political change by checking whether multiple, sustained hostile causes are aligned over time; single shocks or transient changes are unlikely to supplant deeply embedded republican habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of legislative instability
rubrics_metrics.description: Instability that modifies secondary laws (common and compatible with settled society) versus instability that shakes the foundations of the Constitution (always followed by troubles and revolutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate routine, frequent changes in administrative or secondary law from fundamental constitutional instability; the former does not imply systemic collapse, the latter does and should be treated as a distinct danger sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of rapid descent into despotism after loss of republican institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When republican institutions are lost, a democratic republic is likely to pass quickly to despotism rather than a long-living limited monarchy, because elected magistrates' powers can transfer to a hereditary or unchecked sovereign and habits of unbounded magistracy may persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate transitions away from republicanism with particular concern: patterns of concentrated arbitrary power and erosion of responsibility among magistrates can presage an abrupt slide into despotism rather than a gradual monarchical phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability of home-grown aristocracy in democratic societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracies historically arise through conquest and imposed inequality; a people originating in civilization and democracy will not by free will create an aristocracy with inviolable privileges—inequality as a legislative foundation must be extorted, not freely adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the likelihood of entrenched aristocratic elites forming within a democratic society, look for evidence of forceful imposition of inequality, legal codification of privilege, or social mechanisms that prevent mobility; absent these, aristocracy is unlikely to arise organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial prosperity stems from moral and intellectual qualities, not just physical advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Although America has favorable coasts and ports, Tocqueville argues the commercial superiority of Anglo-Americans is 'less attributable... to physical circumstances than to moral and intellectual causes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate national commercial strength by examining cultural traits—risk-tolerance, enterprise, generalist skillsets, adaptability—rather than relying solely on geographic or material endowments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-taking, continuous navigation and speed as sources of lower trading costs
rubrics_metrics.description: American merchants trade at lower rates because they adopt riskier, faster practices (sailing in storms, fewer port calls, continuous progress) which, despite higher losses, reduce travel time and thus lower per-unit costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing comparative commercial efficiency, consider operational practices (willingness to accept higher risk and hardship to shorten voyage times) that can produce cheaper services even if capital or wages are not lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad, generalist capacities and low specialization foster adaptability and innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because division of labor is less extreme, Americans often practice multiple trades, which may reduce perfection in any single craft but 'awakens the intelligence of the workman' and expands the circle of his capacities—enabling easy occupational shifts and innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess human-capital advantages not only by depth of specialization but by breadth and flexibility; in dynamic environments, generalist skills that permit switching occupations and experimenting with methods can be a commercial strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural valorization of novelty linked to improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the idea of novelty is indissolubly connected with the idea of amelioration; constant motion and appetite for new attempts make innovation culturally desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a society's propensity for progress, look for cultural norms that equate novelty with improvement and that socially reward experimentation and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durable commercial prosperity requires naval (sea) power
rubrics_metrics.description: No commercial prosperity can be durable if it cannot be united, in case of need, to naval force; commerce must be backed by capability to protect shipping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess long-term commercial security by asking whether commercial interests are supported by the means of defense/projection (here, naval power); lack of such linkage makes prosperity vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic contiguity and shared interests sustain commercial cooperation even if political union dissolves
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Union were dissolved, commercial states (being contiguous and sharing opinions, interests, and manners) would remain united in commerce and could form a maritime power—economic ties and cheapness of service will override national prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the resilience of commercial networks to political fragmentation by checking geographic proximity, identity of interests, cultural similarity, and comparative economic advantage (cheapness) that incentivize continued economic integration.
